paras: The burning of the colored school at Fair Haven, New Jersey, was the destruction by fire of the school house for Black children in Fair Haven, Monmouth County, late on a Wednesday night in February 1881, during a dispute over admitting Black children to the town's new white school. An Associated Press dispatch attributed the fire to Black residents and named a Black suspect, but no arrest was reported. The fire sharpened Fair Haven's "school war," which led to the white school's closing and a state law against excluding children by color.

According to the Associated Press dispatch, trouble began when Black residents insisted that their children had a right to attend the new school built for white children. Some Black pupils were admitted after the colored school closed, but white children stayed away, and the trustees reopened the colored school with a new teacher, whom Black parents told their children not to obey. The dispatch alone reported that "several threats" had been made by Black residents to burn the colored school house.

Late on a Wednesday night, most likely February 23, the colored school house was found on fire. White residents put out the fire, but the roof was soon found burning from a second fire set in the upper loft, and the building burned to the ground. "The crime is attributed to the colored people," the dispatch said; police were searching for Henry Johnson, described as "a negro of bad reputation" seen leaving the building, and a Black man, Henry Curtis, was said to have informed against the "supposed incendiaries." No report of an arrest, a charge or a trial appears in the coverage.

On March 15 a meeting in the white school house, attended by about fifty Black men, took up a proposal to raise $1,500 for a new colored school. Joseph Richardson, a Black resident, demanded a school "as good as the white children have" or an addition to the white school; the whites voted down the addition and carried a separate building.

The dispute had already reached the legislature, which the week before March 22 passed a law penalizing refusal of admission to a child on account of color. On March 21 the school board closed the white school, a step Black residents charged was meant to forestall their demand under the law; the county superintendent said they were "morally bound" not to seek admission but could not legally be refused. On March 30 Black children who went to the white school were turned away, a majority of whites advised the trustees to keep them out "by main force if necessary," and their parents said they would go to court.

The Associated Press dispatch, which the Washington Evening Star headlined "A SCHOOL HOUSE BURNED DOWN BY INCENDIARIES" on February 26 and the Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe, Louisiana, reprinted on March 11, carried the news; Southern editorial paragraphs then treated its attribution as fact. The Alexandria Gazette said the "negroes" had burned their school house "in order to force their children into the white school" and predicted that "the Northern people will learn something about negro character after awhile." The Anderson Intelligencer of South Carolina spoke of "trouble with the colored brother" who had burned his own school.

The Savannah Morning News called the fire "evidently incendiary" without naming anyone, while blaming the school closings on Black parents who "endeavored to force their children into the white schools." New York papers covered the later meetings as a "school war" and "race troubles"; The Sun's Red Bank correspondent mentioned the burning only as the point at which the war "grew fiercer," naming no culprit and quoting Black speakers at length.
The Trenton Sentinel headed its item "JUSTICE WITHOUT REGARD TO RACE" and backed the admission bill, while the Daily Gazette faulted Gen. Clinton B. Fisk for "officiousness in favor of the negro."

Who set the fire is not settled: the Associated Press blamed Black residents, but The Sun and the Savannah Morning News named no one. Accounts also differ on when the white school closed, the Alexandria Gazette reporting it closed by February 28 and the New York dispatches dating the board's action to March 21.

bases: The violence reported is the deliberate burning of the school house for Black children amid a school-admission dispute, by persons the papers did not identify beyond an attribution to Black residents (A1, A7, A15).

The AP dispatch (A1) and The Sun's separate Red Bank correspondent (A7) both report the burning of the colored school house, and Savannah (A15) and Alexandria (A2) also report it; who set it rests on the AP dispatch alone.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Mixed School Row in New Jersey. A SCHOOL HOUSE BURNED DOWN BY INCENDIARIES' over the AP text blaming colored people.
Alexandria Gazette blamed Black residents for the arson and mocked Northern lessons in 'negro character'.
Anderson Intelligencer joked about 'trouble with the colored brother' and stated Black residents burned their own school.
The Sun's 'FAIR HAVEN'S SCHOOL WAR' gave a detailed meeting report quoting Black speakers.
Savannah Morning News called the fire 'evidently incendiary' but blamed the school closings on Black parents.
Trenton Sentinel's 'JUSTICE WITHOUT REGARD TO RACE' condemned excluding colored children and backed the admission bill.
Daily Gazette's 'NEW JERSEY'S WAR OF RACES' faulted Fisk's 'officiousness in favor of the negro'.
